newsitem.title: ITALY: Jovial Pope seems invigorated by mountain break.
newsitem.headline: Jovial Pope seems invigorated by mountain break.

text.p: A jovial Pope John Paul, looking rested and healthy midway through a mountain holiday, joked on Sunday that he wished he could spend more time in the open air and less in Vatican corridors.

The 77-year-old Pontiff, who has had a series of health problems in recent years, made his only scheduled public appearance during the 10-day retreat that began on Wednesday in the Val D'Aosta region near the French border.

"So many times in Rome, and only once here in the Val D'Aosta -- this disproportion can't be changed," he said with a hint of disappointment, referring to the weekly Sunday address and blessing he usually delivers from the Vatican.
The Pope, who years ago complained about the Vatican being "a prison", addressed about 100 people from the balcony of a mountaintop stone and wooden chalet where he is staying.
Aides say the vacation seems to have invigorated him midway through a hectic year in which he has already made four overseas trips and plans two more.

"He is in fine health and good spirits. I think that his spirits are fine even when he is in the Vatican but today he has the good fortune of being in this splendid setting," Chief Vatican Spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said.
The Pope, his face reddened by the sun, has been taking short walks using a cane on day outings in the isolated mountain area, enjoying brief afternoon naps in a tent carried by aides.
From his room in the chalet, adjacent to a church-owned retreat outside the isolated hamlet of Les Combes, the Pope has a view of the snow-capped Mont Blanc and alpine glaciers.
The Vatican says the holiday is strictly private.

Italian and Vatican security men have been keeping reporters, photographers and tourists far from the Pope, whose daily forays are planned by a local mountain expert and kept secret until he has returned to the chalet.
"This may seem like a paradox but even a Pope has a right to a minimum of privacy," Navarro-Valls said.
The outside world has nevertheless intruded. On Sunday the Pope condemned the killing in Spain of politician Miguel Angel Blanco, who was kidnapped by Basque separatist guerrillas.
He deplored the murder as an unjustified "act of blood" and hoped that Spaniards could find the courage and tenacity to seek peaceful coexistence.
"Even while he is trying to rest here, the world with all its sufferings is still present in his mind," Navarro-Valls said.
Navarro-Valls said the Pope has been reading books on anthropology, philosophy and sociology in various languages.
The Pope was an avid mountaineer until he broke his leg in a fall in the Vatican in 1994 and underwent hip replacement surgery. Doctors removed an inflamed appendix 10 months ago.
The Pope broke with centuries of tradition in 1986 when he began taking holidays outside the papal summer retreat at Castelgandolfo, south of Rome. He returns there on Saturday.
